wrong_text: the contraceptive injection (Depo-Provera; effective for 12 weeks)
problem: Depo-Provera lasts 13 weeks, not 12 weeks. NHS states: 'You'll usually need to have an injection once every 12 to 13 weeks' and 'Depo-Provera is most commonly given in the UK and lasts for 13 weeks.' Stating 12 weeks is factually wrong and would cause students to give an incorrect answer. Source: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/contraception/contraceptive-injection/
correction: the contraceptive injection (Depo-Provera; effective for 13 weeks)

wrong_text: The term used for the developing baby from 9 weeks after fertilisation until birth
problem: NHS states the transition from embryo to foetus occurs at 8 weeks of pregnancy (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/week-by-week/1-to-12/8-weeks/). Pregnancy weeks are counted from the last menstrual period, approximately 2 weeks before fertilisation, so 8 weeks of pregnancy equals approximately 6 weeks after fertilisation — not 9 weeks after fertilisation as the lesson states. Saying '9 weeks after fertilisation' corresponds to roughly 11 weeks of pregnancy, which is substantially later than the accepted NHS figure. Students answering exam questions using NHS/clinical sources would give the wrong figure.
correction: The term used for the developing baby from 8 weeks of pregnancy (approximately 6 weeks after fertilisation) until birth, when all major organs are present and further development is growth and maturation.

wrong_text: data-def="The term used for the developing baby from 9 weeks after fertilisation until birth, when all major organs are present and further development is growth and maturation."
problem: Same error as glossary_terms: the inline dfn tooltip repeats the incorrect '9 weeks after fertilisation' figure. NHS says the transition is at 8 weeks of pregnancy (~6 weeks post-fertilisation). Source: https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/week-by-week/1-to-12/8-weeks/
correction: data-def="The term used for the developing baby from 8 weeks of pregnancy (approximately 6 weeks after fertilisation) until birth, when all major organs are present and further development is growth and maturation."

problem: Current NHS and RCOG guidance has revised these figures downward. The NHS now states the miscarriage risk for amniocentesis is 'up to 1 in 200' (0.5%), and for CVS 'less than 1 in 200' for singleton pregnancies (also ~0.5%). The RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 8 (reviewed December 2024) states the additional risk for both procedures by a skilled operator is 'likely to be below 0.5%'. The older '1% amnio / 1-2% CVS' figures overstate the risk and may be misleading for students and parents. The lesson's statement that CVS 'carries a slightly higher miscarriage risk than amniocentesis' is directionally correct but the absolute figures are outdated. Source: https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/amniocentesis/risks/ and https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/chorionic-villus-sampling-cvs/risks/
correction: approximately 0.5% (1 in 200) for amniocentesis, with CVS carrying a similar or marginally higher risk; both are below 1% when performed by a skilled operator according to current RCOG guidance (2024)

field: conclusion_html and key_fact — amniocentesis miscarriage risk
wrong_text: It carries an approximate miscarriage risk of 1%
problem: Same issue as above — the key fact box and conclusion both state a 1% miscarriage risk for amniocentesis. Current NHS guidance says 'up to 1 in 200' (0.5%), not 1 in 100. RCOG 2024 states below 0.5%. The '1%' figure is the older, higher-end estimate and overstates current clinical data. Source: https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/amniocentesis/risks/
correction: It carries an approximate miscarriage risk of up to 0.5% (1 in 200) according to current NHS guidance

wrong_text: Women are advised to take 400 micrograms (mcg) of folic acid every day from at least one month before conception
problem: Current NHS guidance (https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/trying-for-a-baby/planning-your-pregnancy/) says women should take folic acid 'as soon as you start trying for a baby, ideally for 3 months before'. The lesson's 'at least one month' was the older minimum recommendation. The current NHS primary advice is 3 months (approximately 12 weeks) before conception to ensure adequate stores are built up before the neural tube forms. Understating the recommended lead time may cause students to give an out-of-date answer and means women reading the content could start supplementation too late.
correction: Women are advised to take 400 micrograms (mcg) of folic acid every day ideally for 3 months before conception (and continuing until 12 weeks pregnant)

wrong_text: Women planning a pregnancy should take 400 micrograms of folic acid daily, starting at least one month before conception and continuing through the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.
problem: Same as above — 'at least one month before' is the old minimum; current NHS primary recommendation is 'ideally 3 months before'. The key fact box is particularly prominent and will be the main thing students learn. Source: https://www.nhs.uk/pregnancy/trying-for-a-baby/planning-your-pregnancy/
correction: Women planning a pregnancy should take 400 micrograms of folic acid daily, ideally starting 3 months before conception and continuing through the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.
